CHAPTER V

NUMERICAL APPROXIMATIONS TO FRACTIONAL
PROBLEMS OF THE CALCULUS OF VARIATIONS
AND OPTIMAL CONTROL

Shakoor Pooseh*, Ricardo Almeida† and Delfim F. M. Torres‡
Center for Research and Development in Mathematics and Applications (CIDMA)
Department of Mathematics, University of Aveiro, 3810-193 Aveiro, Portugal

**Keywords:** fractional calculus of variations, fractional optimal control, numerical methods, direct methods, indirect methods

**AMS Subject Classification:** 49K05, 49M25, 26A33

1. INTRODUCTION

A fractional problem of the calculus of variations and optimal control consists in the study of an optimization problem in which the objective functional or constraints depend on derivatives and integrals of arbitrary, real or complex, orders. This is a generalization of the classical theory, where derivatives and integrals can only appear in integer orders.

1.1. Preliminaries

Integer order derivatives and integrals have a unified meaning in the literature. In contrast, there are several different approaches and definitions in fractional calculus for derivatives and integrals of arbitrary order. The following definitions and notations will be used throughout this chapter. See [19].

**Definition 1.1 (Gamma function).** The Euler integral of the second kind

\[\Gamma(z) = \int_{0}^{\infty} t^{z-1} e^{-t} dt, \quad Re(z) > 0,\]

is called the gamma function.

using it as a cover leaf.Definition 1.5 (Riemann–Liouville fractional derivative). Let $x(\cdot)$ be an absolutely continuous function in $[a,b]$, $x(\cdot) \in AC[a,b]$, and $0 \leq \alpha < 1$.

The left Riemann–Liouville fractional derivative of order $\alpha$ is given by
$$a{D}_t^\alpha x(t) = \frac{1}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)} \frac{d}{dt} \int_a^t (t-\tau)^{-\alpha} x(\tau) d\tau, \quad t \in [a,b].$$ 

The right Riemann–Liouville fractional derivative of order $\alpha$ is given by
$$t{D}_b^\alpha x(t) = \frac{1}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)} \left(-\frac{d}{dt} \right) \int_t^b (\tau-t)^{-\alpha} x(\tau) d\tau, \quad t \in [a,b].$$

Another type of fractional derivatives, introduced by Caputo, is closely related to the Riemann–Liouville definitions.

Definition 1.6 (Caputo’s fractional derivative). For a function $x(\cdot) \in AC[a,b]$ with $0 \leq \alpha < 1$:

The left Caputo fractional derivative of order $\alpha$ is given by
$$c{_D}_t^\alpha x(t) = \frac{1}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)} \int_a^t (t-\tau)^{-\alpha} \dot{x}(\tau) d\tau, \quad t \in [a,b].$$

The right Caputo fractional derivative of order $\alpha$ is given by
$$t{D}_b^\alpha x(t) = \frac{-1}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)} \int_t^b (\tau-t)^{-\alpha} \dot{x}(\tau) d\tau, \quad t \in [a,b].$$

Definition 1.7 (Hadamard fractional integral). Let $x: [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$.

The left Hadamard fractional integral of order $\alpha > 0$ is defined by
$$a_x^\alpha x(t) = \frac{1}{\Gamma(\alpha)} \int_a^t \left(\ln \frac{t}{\tau}\right)^{-\alpha-1} \frac{x(\tau)}{\tau} d\tau, \quad t \in [a,b].$$

The right Hadamard fractional integral of order $\alpha > 0$ is defined by
$$t{x_b^\alpha} x(t) = \frac{1}{\Gamma(\alpha)} \int_t^b \left(\ln \frac{\tau}{t}\right)^{-\alpha-1} \frac{x(\tau)}{\tau} d\tau, \quad t \in [a,b].$$

When $\alpha = m$ is an integer, these fractional integrals are $m$-fold integrals:
$$a_x^m x(t) = \int_a^t \frac{d\tau_1}{\tau_1} \int_a^{\tau_1} \ldots \int_a^{\tau_{m-1}} \frac{x(\tau_m)}{\tau_m} d\tau_m,$$
and
$$t{x_b^m} x(t) = \int_b^t \frac{d\tau_1}{\tau_1} \int_{\tau_1}^b \frac{d\tau_2}{\tau_2} \ldots \int_{\tau_{m-1}}^b \frac{x(\tau_m)}{\tau_m} d\tau_m.$$

For a function $x(\cdot) \in AC[a,b]$ with $0 \leq \alpha \leq 1$, the left and right Caputo and Hadamard fractional integrals are differential-, differential-differential-, and differential-differential-integral orders of $x(\cdot)$ from $[a,b]$.

When $\alpha = m$ is an integer along with $-1 \leq \beta \leq 0$, let the fractional integrals are $m$-fold integrals of orders:
$$\alpha {x_b^\beta}_x(t) = \int_a^t \frac{d\tau_1}{\tau_1} \int_a^{\tau_1} \ldots \int_a^{\tau_{m-1}} \frac{x(\tau_m)}{\tau_m} d\tau_m,$$
and
$$\beta x_b^\beta x(t) = \int_b^t \frac{d\tau_1}{\tau_1} \int_{\tau_1}^b \frac{d\tau_2}{\tau_2} \ldots \int_{\tau_{m-1}}^b \frac{x(\tau_m)}{\tau_m} d\tau_m.$$

The reasoning used to prove these integrals may be found in mathnasium books.

产品成本等参数, 菜单类型等参数, 维度等信息。然后我们使用Spark SQL分析和处理该数据。这张图展示了in-coming函数的输入维度、输出维度以及对应的分布。从图中可以看出, 该函数接受一个以商品 id 作为键的dict类型参数, 并将该商品作为key输出, 一个以商品 id 作为键的dict类型的参数, 并根据dict类型计算指数(这个计算被输入值下标入, 并将其转换为输入新的输出维度)。然后我们再对这个输出的结果乘以一个特定数值, 如超过 1 后终止。下面是一个示例, 这个函数通过预测 bedtime_hour 变量, 从而实现对 bedtime 变量的控制。若 bedtime_hour 的值很低, 则说明夜间活动次数低；若高出给定范围内, 则说明夜间活动次数高, 反之。对于 sleep_power 我们则指定一个固定值, 即计算睡眠持续时间 (power)。 ess_sleep 这个参数指定了长时间度量 (20、40 和 60 min) 的条件覆盖。当 ess_sleep 等于为长时 (低于 20 min), 则只会覆盖短时 (低于 20 min), 也不会覆盖介于 20 与 40 min 之间的时间标签；如果 ess_sleep 等于为短时 (大于 60 min), 则仅通过计算总睡眠时间覆盖从短到长的时间标签。

where \( \alpha \in (0,1) \) is a fixed parameter.

The functional representation of a NN approximation using fractional derivatives is as follows:

$$

x(t) = { \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} ( -1 ) ^ {k} x^{(k)}( t - \tau ) \over k! (1 - \alpha ) \Gamma ( 1 - \alpha )}, \quad t \in [t_a, t_b] , \quad t \in \langle a, b \rangle \\

$$

where \( x^{(k)} \) is the k-th derivative of the function \( x \) defined on \( [ t_a, t_b ] \) and \( x^{(k)}( t ) \) is its k-th derivative itself.

The approximation of \( x(t) \) by a TF neural network with the ReLU activation function is given by the following expression:

$$

x(t) = { \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} ( -1 ) ^ {k} x^{(k)}( t - \tau ) \over k! ( - \alpha ) \Gamma ( 1 + \alpha )} {e \over \alpha - 1 t^{\alpha} \Gamma(1 + \alpha)}, \quad t \in [t_a, t_b].\\

$$

The approximation error is defined as:

$$

|| x(t) - { \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} ( -1 ) ^ {k} x^{(k)}( t - \tau ) \over k! ( 1 - \alpha ) \Gamma ( 1 - \alpha )} { e \over \alpha - 1 t^{\alpha} \Gamma(1 + \alpha)} | dt \|,

$$

where \( ||\cdot|| \) denotes the 2-norm.

To train the neural network, the following optimization problem is solved:

$$

arg\ min \limits _ \alpha \| e \over \alpha - 1 t^{\alpha} \Gamma(1 + \alpha) ||,\quad s.t.\quad | \alpha \in (0,1], \quad t \in [t_a, t_b], \\

$$

where \( e \in \mathbb{R}^N \) is the vector of residual errors, \( f{:}[t_a,t_b]\to \mathbb{R}^N \) is the vector of residual errors, and \( \Gamma(\cdot) \) is the gamma function.

To train the network, the loss function \( L = || e \over \alpha - 1 t^{\alpha} \Gamma(1 + \alpha) ||^2 \) is minimized.

To find the optimal model, the gradient descent method is applied:

$$

\alpha^{t+1} = \alpha^t + \eta(t) \vec{\nabla} L = \alpha^t - 1 \eta(t) \Gamma( 1 + \alpha) \vec{E}_a, \quad t \in [t_a, t_b] \\ \quad (\vec{E}_a) = {1 \over N} \sum_{j=0}^{N-1} (s^{(j+1)}(t)-\alpha \,t - (\alpha-1) \xi_jx^{(j)}(t-\tau)^{\alpha}), \quad t \in [t_a, t_b]. \\

$$

with \( s^{(j)}(t) \) and \(x^{(j)}(t-\tau)\) being the derivatives of the neural network given by

$$s^{(j)}(t) = \sum_{k \le j} (-1)^k \frac{t^{(j+1)} (\tau)}{\Gamma(j+1)} x^{(j+k)} (t),$$

and

$$x^{(j+1)}(t-\tau)=\sum_{k=j+1}^{\infty}(-1)^k\frac{(t-\tau)^{(k)}}{\Gamma(k)}\Gamma(j+1).$$

.1.2.2 Approximating Using Moments of a Function

By moments of a function, we have no physical or distributive sense in mind. The naming comes from the fact that, during expansion, the terms of the form

\[
V_p(t) := V_p(x(t)) = (1-p) \int_a^t (\tau - \alpha)^{p-2}x(\tau)d\tau, \quad p \in \mathbb{N}, \quad \tau \geq a, \tag{10}
\]

resemble the formulas of central moments (cf. [8]). We assume that \( V_p(x(\cdot)) \), \( p \in \mathbb{N} \), denotes the \( (p-2)th \) moment of a function \( x(\cdot) \in AC^2[a,b] \).

The following lemma, that is given here without a proof, is the key relation to extract an expansion formula for Riemann–Liouville derivatives.

Lemma 2.3 (cf. Lemma 2.12 of [12]). Let \( x(\cdot) \in AC[a,b] \) and \( 0 < \alpha < 1 \). Then the left Riemann–Liouville fractional derivative, \( {_aD_t} \alpha x(\cdot) \), exists almost everywhere in \( [a,b] \). Moreover, \( {_aD_t} \alpha x(\cdot) \in L_p[a,b] \) for \( 1 \leq p < \frac{1}{\alpha} \) and

\[
{_aD_t}\alpha x(t) = \frac{1}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)} \left[ \frac{x(a)}{(t-a)^\alpha} + \int_a^t (t-\tau)^{-\alpha} x(\tau)d\tau \right], \quad t \in (a,b). \tag{11}
\]

The same argument is valid for the right Riemann–Liouville derivative and

\[
{_tD_t} \alpha x(t) = \frac{1}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)} \left[ \frac{x(b)}{(b-t)^\alpha} - \int_t^b (\tau-t)^{-\alpha} \dot{x}(\tau)d\tau \right], \quad t \in (a,b). \tag{12}
\]

Theorem 2.4 (cf. [7]). With the same assumptions of Lemma 2.3, the left Riemann–Liouville derivative can be expanded as

\[
{_aD_t} \alpha x(t) = \frac{(t-a)^{-\alpha}}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)} x(t) + B(\alpha)(t-a)^{1-\alpha} \dot{x}(t)
- \sum_{p=2}^\infty \left[ C(\alpha,p)(t-a)^{1-p-\alpha} V_p(t) - \frac{\Gamma(p-1+\alpha)}{\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(1-\alpha)(p-1)!} (t-a)^{-\alpha} x(t) \right], \tag{13}
\]

where \( V_p(t) \) is defined by (10) and

\[
B(\alpha) = \frac{1}{\Gamma(2-\alpha)} \left( 1 + \sum_{p=1}^\infty \frac{\Gamma(p-1+\alpha)}{\Gamma(\alpha-1)p!} \right),
\]

\[
C(\alpha,p) = \frac{1}{\Gamma(2-\alpha)\Gamma(\alpha-1)} \frac{\Gamma(p-1+\alpha)}{(p-1)!}.
\]

Proof. Integration by parts on the right-hand-side of (11) gives

\[
{_{aD_t} \alpha} x(t) = \frac{x(a)}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)} (t-a)^{-\alpha} + \frac{\dot{x}(a)}{\Gamma(2-\alpha)} (t-a)^{1-\alpha}
+ \frac{1}{\Gamma(2-\alpha)} \int_a^t (t-\tau)^{1-\alpha} \ddot{x}(\tau)d\tau. \tag{13}
\]

.As before, a numerical approximation is achieved by taking only a finite number of terms in the series (12). We approximate the fractional derivative as

\[
aD_t^{\alpha}x(t) \approx A(t-a)^{-\alpha}x(t) + B(t-a)^{1-\alpha}\dot{x}(t) - \sum_{p=2}^{N} C(\alpha, p)(t-a)^{1-p-\alpha}V_p(t),
\]

(15)

where \(A = A(\alpha, N)\) and \(B = B(\alpha, N)\) are given by

\[
A(\alpha, N) = \frac{1}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)} \left( 1 + \sum_{p=2}^{N} \frac{\Gamma(p-1+\alpha)}{\Gamma(\alpha)(p-1)!} \right),
\]

(16)

\[
B(\alpha, N) = \frac{1}{\Gamma(2-\alpha)} \left( 1 + \sum_{p=1}^{N} \frac{\Gamma(p-1+\alpha)}{\Gamma(\alpha-1)p!} \right).
\]

(17)

**Remark 2.5.** This expansion has been proposed in [14] and a simplification has been made in [8], which uses the fact that the infinite series \(\sum_{p=1}^{\infty} \frac{\Gamma(p-1+\alpha)}{\Gamma(\alpha-1)p!}\) tends to \(-1\), and concludes that \(B(\alpha) = 0\), and thus

\[
aD_t^{\alpha}x(t) \approx A(\alpha, N)t^{-\alpha}x(t) - \sum_{p=2}^{N} C(\alpha, p)t^{1-p-\alpha}V_p(t).
\]

(18)

In practice, however, we only use a finite number of terms in series. Therefore,

\[
1 + \sum_{p=1}^{N} \frac{\Gamma(p-1+\alpha)}{\Gamma(\alpha-1)p!} \neq 0,
\]

and we keep here the approximation in the form of equation (15). [3]. To be more precise, the values of \(B(\alpha, N)\), for different choices of \(N\) and \(\alpha\), are given in Table 1. It shows that even for a large \(N\), when \(\alpha\) tends to one, \(B(\alpha, N)\) cannot be ignored.

\]

Extracting the first term of the infinite sum, simplifications and another integration by parts using \(u = (\ln \frac{\tau}{a})^p\), \(du = (p) \frac{1}{\tau} (\ln \frac{\tau}{a})^{p-1}\) and \(dv = [\dot{x}(\tau) + \tau \ddot{x}(\tau)] d\tau\), \(v = \tau \dot{x}(\tau)\) yields

2.4. Error Analysis

When we approximate an infinite series by a finite sum, the choice of the order of approximation is a key question. Having an estimate knowledge of truncation errors, one can choose properly up to which order the approximations should be made to suit the accuracy requirements. In this section we study the errors of the approximations presented so far.

Separating an error term in (8) concludes in

\[

Basic idea of this method is that instead of considering the values of a functional

\[
J[x(\cdot)] = \int_a^b L(t, x(t), \dot{x}(t)) dt
\]

with boundary conditions \(x(a) = x_a\) and \(x(b) = x_b\), on arbitrary admissible curves, we only track the values at an \(n + 1\) grid points, \(t_i\), \(i = 0, \ldots, n\), of the interested time interval [29]. The functional \(J[x(\cdot)]\) is then transformed into a function \(\Psi(x(t_1), x(t_2), \ldots, x(t_{n-1}))\) of the values of unknown function on mesh points. Assuming \(h = t_i - t_{i-1}\), \(x(t_i) = x_i\) and \(\dot{x}_i \approx \frac{x_{i-1} - x_i}{h}\), one has

\[
J[x(\cdot)] \approx \Psi(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_{n-1}) = h \sum_{i=1}^n L(t_i, x_i, \frac{x_i - x_{i-1}}{h}) ,
\]

with the derivative $\dot{x}_i = x_{i+1} - x_i$
The desired values of \(x_i\), \(i = 1, \ldots, n-1\), are the extremum of the multi-variable function with the solution to the system

\[
\frac{\partial \Psi}{\partial x_i} = 0 ,\quad i = 1, \ldots, n - 1.
\]

The fact that only two terms in the sum, \((i-1)\)th and \(i\)th, depend on \(x_i\), makes it rather easy to find the extremum of \(\Psi\) solving a system of algebraic equations. For each \(n\), we obtain a polygonal line which is an approximate solution of the original problem. It has been shown that passing to the limit as \(h \to 0\), the linear system corresponding to finding the extremum of \(\Psi\) is equivalent to the Euler-Lagrange equation of the problem.

**3.1.1. Finite Differences for Fractional Derivatives**

In classical theory, given a derivative of a certain order, \(x^{(n)}\), there is a finite difference approximation of the form

\[
x^{(n)}(t) = \lim_{h \to 0^+} \frac{1}{h^n} \sum_{k=0}^n (-1)^k \binom{n}{k} x(t - kh),
\]

where \(\binom{n}{k}\) is the binomial coefficient and

\[
\binom{n}{k} = \frac{n(n-1)(n-2) \cdots (n-k+1)}{k!} ,\quad n, k \in \mathbb{N}.
\]

The Grünwald–Letnikov definition of fractional derivative is a generalization of this formula to derivatives of arbitrary order.

The series in (2) and (3), the Grünwald–Letnikov definitions, converge absolutely and uniformly if \(x(\cdot)\) is bounded. The infinite sums, backward differences for the left and forward differences for the right derivative in the Grünwald–Letnikov definitions for fractional derivatives, reveals that the arbitrary order derivative of a function at a time \(t\) depends on all values of that function in \((-\infty, t]\) and \([t, \infty)\), for left and right derivatives respectively. This is due to the non-local property of fractional derivatives.

**Theorem 3.6.** The Euler-like method for a fractional variational problem of the form (4) is equivalent to the fractional Euler–Lagrange equation

\frac{\partial L}{\partial x} + t D_t^{\alpha} \frac{\partial L}{\partial_a D_t^{\alpha}x} = 0,

as the mesh size, \(h\), tends to zero.

**Proof.** Consider a minimizer \((x_1, \dots, x_{n-1})\) of \(\Psi\), a variation function \(\eta \in C[a, b]\) with \(\eta(a) = \eta(b) = 0\) and define \(\eta_i = \eta(t_i)\), for \(i = 0, \dots, n\). We remark that \(\eta_0 = \eta_n = 0\) and that \((x_1 + \epsilon t_1, \dots, x_{n-1} + \epsilon t_{n-1})\) is a variation of \((x_1, \dots, x_{n-1})\), with \(|\epsilon| < r\), for some fixed \(r > 0\). Therefore, since \((x_1, \dots, x_{n-1})\) is a minimizer for \(\Psi\), proceeding with Taylor’s expansion, we deduce that

0 \leq \Psi(x_1 + \epsilon t_1, \dots, x_{n-1} + \epsilon t_{n-1}) - \Psi(x_1, \dots, x_{n-1})
= \epsilon \sum_{i=1}^{n} h \left[ \frac{\partial L}{\partial x} [i] \eta_i + \frac{\partial L}{\partial_a D_t^{\alpha}(i)} [i] \frac{\partial L}{\partial_a D_t^{\alpha}(i)} \sum_{k=0}^{i} (\omega_k^{\alpha} \eta_i-k) + O(\epsilon) \right],

where \([\cdot]\) is the operator delimited by the Taylor's expansion, and:

[\partial_i] = \left( t_i, x_i, \frac{1}{h^\alpha} \sum_{k=0}^{i} (\omega_k^\alpha)x_i-k \right).

Since \(\epsilon\) takes any value, it follows that

\sum_{i=1}^{n} h \left[ \frac{\partial L}{\partial x} [i] \eta_i + \frac{\partial L}{\partial_a D_t^{\alpha}(i)} [i] \sum_{k=0}^{i} (\omega_k^\alpha) \eta_i-k \right] = 0. \qquad (29)

On the other hand, since \(\eta_0 = 0\), reordering the terms of the sum, it follows immediately that

\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{\partial L}{\partial_a D_t^{\alpha}[i]} \sum_{k=0}^{i} (\omega_k^\alpha) \eta_i-k = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{\partial L}{\partial_a D_t^{\alpha}(i)} \lambda_i = \int_{0}^{1} \frac{\partial L}{\partial_a D_t^{\alpha}(i)} \lambda_i \, dx
= \sum_{i=1}^{n} \eta_i \frac{\partial L}{\partial_a D_t^{\alpha}(i)} \lambda_i. \qquad (30)

Substituting this relation into equation (29), we obtain

\sum_{i=1}^{n} \eta_i h \left[ \frac{\partial L}{\partial x} [i] + \frac{1}{h^{\alpha}} \sum_{k=0}^{n-i} (\omega_k^\alpha) \frac{\partial L}{\partial_a D_t^{\alpha}} (i+k) \right] = 0.

Since \(\eta_i\) is arbitrary, for \(i = 1, \dots, n-1\), we deduce that

\frac{\partial L}{\partial x} [i] + \frac{1}{h^{\alpha}} \sum_{k=0}^{n-i} (\omega_k^\alpha) \frac{\partial L}{\partial_a D_t^{\alpha}} (i+k) = 0, \quad \text{for } i = 1, \dots, n-1.

.Let us study the case when \(n\) goes to infinity. Let \(\overline{t} \in ]a, b[\) and \(i \in \{1, \ldots, n\}\) such that \(t_{i-1} < \overline{t} \leq t_i\). First observe that, in such case, we also have \(i \to \infty\) and \(n-i \to \infty\). In fact, let \(i \in \{1, \ldots, n\}\) be such that

\[a + (i-1)h < \overline{t} \leq a + ih.\]

So, \(i < (\overline{t} - a)/h + 1\), which implies that

\[n - i > n\frac{b - \overline{t}}{b - a} - 1.\]

Then

\[\lim_{n \to \infty, i \to \infty} t_i = \overline{t}.\]

Assume that there exists a function \(\overline{x} \in C[a, b]\) satisfying

\[\forall \epsilon > 0 \exists N \forall n \geq N : |x_i - \overline{x}(t_i)| < \epsilon, \quad \forall i = 1, \ldots, n - 1.\]

As \(\overline{x}\) is uniformly continuous, we have

\[\forall \epsilon > 0 \exists N \forall n \geq N : |x_i - \overline{x}(\overline{t})| < \epsilon, \quad \forall i = 1, \ldots, n - 1.\]

By the continuity assumption of \(\overline{x}\), we deduce that

\[
\lim_{n \to \infty, i \to \infty} \frac{1}{h^\alpha} \sum_{k=0}^{n-i} (\omega_k^\alpha) \frac{\partial L}{\partial a} D_t^\alpha [i + k] = t D_b^\alpha \frac{\partial L}{\partial a} (\overline{t}, \overline{x}(\overline{t}), a D_t^\alpha \overline{x}(\overline{t})).
\]

For \(n\) sufficiently large (and therefore \(i\) also sufficiently large),

\[\lim_{n \to \infty, i \to \infty} \frac{\partial L}{\partial x} [i] = \frac{\partial L}{\partial x} (\overline{t}, \overline{x}(\overline{t}), a D_t^\alpha \overline{x}(\overline{t})).\]

In conclusion,

\[\frac{\partial L}{\partial x} (\overline{t}, \overline{x}(\overline{t}), a D_t^\alpha \overline{x}(\overline{t})) + t D_b^\alpha \frac{\partial L}{\partial a} (\overline{t}, \overline{x}(\overline{t}), a D_t^\alpha \overline{x}(\overline{t})) = 0. \qquad (30)\]

Using the continuity condition, we prove that the fractional Euler–Lagrange equation (30) holds for all values on the closed interval \(a \leq t \leq b\). 

### 3.1.3. Examples

Now we apply the Euler-like direct method to some test problems for which the exact solutions are known. Although we propose problems for the interval \([0, 1]\), moving to arbitrary intervals is only a matter of more computations. To measure the errors related to approximations, different norms can be used. Since a direct method seeks for the function values at certain points, we use the maximum norm to determine how close we can get to the exact value at that point. Assume that the exact value of the function \(x(\cdot)\), at the point \(t_i\), is \(x(t_i)\) and it is approximated by \(x_i\). The error is defined as

\[E = \max\{|x(t_i) - x_i|, \ i = 1, \ldots, n - 1\}.\]

transition function describing movement of material point.As in the classical case, indirect methods in fractional sense provide the necessary conditions of optimality using the first variation. Fractional Euler–Lagrange equations are now a well-known and well-studied subject in fractional calculus. For a simple problem of the form (4), following [1], a necessary condition implies that the solution must satisfy a fractional boundary value differential equation.

Theorem 4.1 (cf. [1]. Let $x(\cdot)$ have a continuous left Riemann–Liouville derivative of order $\alpha$ and $J$ be a functional of the form

$$J[x(\cdot)] = \int_a^b L(t, x(t), _a D_t^\alpha x(t))dt \quad (37)$$

subject to the boundary conditions $x(a) = x_a$ and $x(b) = x_b$. Then a necessary condition for $J$ to have an extremum for a function $x(\cdot)$ is that $x(\cdot)$ satisfies the following Euler-Lagrange equation:

$$\left\{
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial L}{\partial x} + _{t} D_b^\alpha \frac{\partial L}{\partial x^\alpha} = 0, \\
x(a) = x_a, \quad x(b) = x_b,
\end{aligned}
\right. \quad (38)$$

which is called the fractional Euler–Lagrange equation.

Proof. Assume that $x^*(t)$ is the desired function and let $x(t) = x^*(t) + \varepsilon \eta(t)$ be a family of curves that satisfy boundary conditions, i.e., $\eta(a) = \eta(b) = 0$. Since $a D_t^\alpha$ is a linear operator, for any $x(\cdot)$, the functional becomes

$$J[x(\cdot)] = \int_a^b L(t, x^*(t) + \varepsilon \eta(t), _a D_t^\alpha x^*(t) + \varepsilon \alpha D_t^\alpha \eta(t))dt, \quad (39)$$

which is a function of $\varepsilon$, $J[\varepsilon]$. Since $J$ assumes its extremum at $\varepsilon = 0$, one has $\frac{dJ}{d\varepsilon} \big|_{\varepsilon = 0} = 0$, i.e.,

$$\int_a^b \left( \frac{\partial L}{\partial x}\eta + \frac{\partial L}{\partial _a D_t^\alpha} _a D_t^\alpha \eta \right) dt = 0. \quad (40)$$

Using the fractional integration by parts of the form

$$\int_a^b g(t)_a D_t^\alpha f(t)dt = \int_a^b f(t)_t D_b^\alpha g(t)dt, \quad (41)$$

on the second term and applying the fundamental theorem of the calculus of variations completes the proof. 

Remark 4.2. Many variants of this theorem can be found in the literature. Different types of fractional terms have been embedded in the Lagrangian and appropriate versions of Euler–Lagrange equations have been derived using proper integration by parts formulas. See [1, 3, 6, 22, 24] for details.

\]

\[\
\begin{align*}
\operatorname{min} \quad \tilde{J}[x(\cdot)) = & \int_{0}^{1} \left[ A t^{-\alpha} x(t) + B t^{1-\alpha} \dot{x}(t) - \sum_{p=2}^{N} C_p t^{1-p-\alpha} V_p(t) - 1 \right] dt, \\
& \dot{V}_p(t) = (1-p)t^{p-2} x(t), \quad p = 2, \ldots, N, \\
& V_p(0) = 0, \quad p = 2, \ldots, N, \\
& x(0) = 0, \quad x(1) = \frac{1}{\Gamma(\alpha + 1)}.
\end{align*}
\ (46)\]

Following the classical optimal control approach of Pontryagin [26], this time with

\[

\]
